## 0. Purpose & scope

This is a shared dictionary for the terms used across the Worklode specs. Each
spec explains a term in depth where it matters most; this page gives the short,
plain-language version so a reader does not need to hunt through every spec to
follow along. When a definition here and a definition in another spec seem to
disagree, the other spec is the authority — this page just points you there.

Terms are grouped by the part of the system they belong to. Within a group,
they're in the order a newcomer would meet them, not alphabetically.

**In scope:** plain-language definitions of the entities, states, and edge
types defined by specs 004, 005, 006, 007, 025, 026, and the `ns/` ontology
files that back them.

**Out of scope:** CLI command syntax and flags (see the relevant spec or run
`lode help`), and terms specific to a single narrow feature that only that
feature's spec needs.

## 1. The execution backbone

The **backbone** (spec 004) is the database that holds the facts about work:
who is doing what, and what state it's in. It's the source of truth agents and
people read from and write to while they work.

**Task.** One unit of work that can be picked up, worked, and finished. Every
task has a **kind** — `feature` (new capability), `bug` (fix wrong behavior),
`chore` (maintenance with no behavior change), `design` (write or revise a
design document), `review` (review someone else's work), or `spike`
(time-boxed experiment whose output gets thrown away). A task also has a
**priority** (`critical`, `high`, `medium`, or `low`).

**Worktree.** A separate, isolated copy of a git repository's working files,
checked out on its own branch. Worklode uses one worktree per task in
progress, so agents working different tasks never step on each other's
uncommitted changes.

**Lease.** A claim that ties one task to one worktree for as long as work is
in progress. Only the worktree holding the lease may update that task.

**Claim.** The action of taking an unclaimed, ready task and leasing it to a
worktree, done as a single all-or-nothing database transaction so two agents
can never claim the same task at once.

**Event log.** An append-only record of everything that has happened to a
task or document — created, claimed, delivered, reopened, and so on. Nothing
is ever edited or deleted from it, so it doubles as the audit trail: you can
always answer "what happened, and when."

**Edge.** A typed link between two tasks (or two documents). The backbone
defines four:
- **`blocks`** — one task must finish before another can start.
- **`child_of`** — one task is a piece of a larger task; a task with children
  is a container by virtue of having them, not because it was declared as one.
- **`follow_up_to`** — one task was split off from work on another.
- **`duplicate_of`** — one task is the same request as another, which is the
  one to actually work.

**Ranking and pickup** (spec 005) decide *which* ready task an agent should
claim next, out of everything that's claimable. **Focus** narrows that choice
to a specific area (a project, a component); **concern** further narrows it to
a category of problem the agent is looking for (e.g. completeness).
**`--strict-focus`** refuses to fall back outside the named focus even when
nothing there is ready. **`needs-decomposition`** flags a task that is too
large to work directly and should be broken into child tasks first.

## 2. Design documents

Worklode treats specs, ADRs (architecture decision records), and plans as
first-class, trackable documents (spec 025), collectively called
**DesignDocs**.

**Spec.** A document that states an intent meant to stay true after it's
built — a description of how something should work. A spec is what "drift"
(§4) gets checked against.

**ADR.** An architecture decision record: a spec that records one specific
decision and the reasoning behind it, rather than describing a whole system.

**Plan.** An executable document: a set of task definitions plus the
instructions for doing them. Accepting a plan mints one real task per task
definition it declares. A plan is spent once its tasks are all done — it
carries no lasting truth of its own, only the specs it points back to.

**Section.** An addressable, individually linkable part of a spec or ADR,
identified by a stable anchor (like `#sec-4.2`) that never changes for the
life of the document, even as the document is revised.

**Status.** A document's place in its lifecycle: `draft` (being written, or
under review with the review not yet settled), `accepted` (approved as
intent), or `superseded` (replaced, in whole or in part, by a later document).

**Covers.** A plan's promise to see a given spec section actually built. A
plan can cover a section fully (nothing more is owed once it executes),
partially (only part of the section), or declare it covers none of a section
it's still bound by — recorded so that omission reads as a deliberate choice,
not an oversight.

**Defers.** A plan's explicit handoff of a section it deliberately will not
build, naming the other document expected to cover it instead. This keeps a
section that's simply someone else's job from showing up as "unplanned."

**Amend / supersede.** Two ways a later document can change an earlier one's
meaning without erasing history. Amending adds to or adjusts what a section
says; superseding replaces it outright. Either way, the original text and its
section number stay put — you follow the amendment or replacement forward
from it, never renumber the original.

## 3. The knowledge graph

The **knowledge graph** (spec 006) is a queryable graph view built by
projecting facts out of the backbone and other sources (git hosting, CI,
deploys). It's where you ask questions that span many tasks and documents at
once, such as "which parts of the codebase have no owning spec?"

**Component.** A software part — usually a directory or package — that is the
smallest unit the knowledge graph reasons about ownership and coverage for.

**Deliverable.** A declared definition of done: the point where a spec's
intent is checked against something concrete that actually exists, such as a
running system in a known state.

**Effect.** A tolerated deviation from what a spec says should be true, named
so that drift queries know to ignore it instead of flagging it as a problem.
An **AcceptedDeviation** is the record of that tolerance: which document
approved treating the gap as expected rather than a bug.

**Drift.** A place where reality (what's actually running or actually in the
code) doesn't match what a spec says should be true. Spec 007 owns how drift
is queried and reported.

**Issue** and **Pull Request.** A tracker ticket and a proposed code change,
each pulled in ("projected") from the hosting provider (e.g. GitHub) and
mirrored to whichever task they relate to.

**Skill.** One org-wide, reusable set of instructions an agent can load before
starting a task — identified by name and the repository it came from.

**Artifact, Build, Deployment, Environment, Commit, Runtime event.** The
pieces of the runtime/deploy side of the graph: an **Artifact** is one built,
versioned unit (a container image, a package, a release); a **Build** is the
CI run that produced it; a **Deployment** is one rollout of an artifact or
commit to a target; an **Environment** is a deployment stage (e.g.
"production"); a **Commit** is one change on a repository's default branch;
and a **Runtime event** is something observed happening to a live deployment,
like a crash loop or an out-of-memory kill.

## 4. Projects and people

**Project.** The umbrella for all the work across a set of repositories —
Worklode's grouping above a single repo.

**Crew.** The time-limited group of people actively working a project — not
every person who has ever touched it, only those currently contributing.
Someone leaves the Crew, and their open work goes through a handoff review
rather than being silently dropped.

**Actor.** Whoever or whatever performed an action — a person or an agent.
Automatic actions taken on a person's behalf are labeled as such, so the
audit trail always distinguishes a human decision from an agent one acting
under it.

**Approval.** A recorded decision that something (a document, a deliverable)
is accepted, tied to who made the call and when.

## 5. Groupings are queries, not rows

Worklode deliberately has very few container-like tables. Most "sets of
things" — a plan's tasks, a milestone's deliverables, a whole project's work —
are computed by asking a question (a query) rather than stored as a group you
add rows to. This keeps the data model small and keeps every grouping
provably in sync with the facts it's built from, instead of a second copy of
the truth that can drift out of date.

**Milestone.** A cross-plan grouping of deliverables that are meant to ship
together — planned for a future version of Worklode, not yet built.

## 6. Reading a cross-reference

A few shorthand patterns show up throughout the specs:

- **`004 §6.1`** means "spec 004, section 6.1."
- **`{#sec-6.1}`** is the anchor a section carries, so a link can point at it
  directly and keep pointing at the same text even if the document around it
  changes.
- **`WL-SPEC-25#sec-9`** is the cross-project shorthand: `WL` is the project
  key, `SPEC-25` means spec number 25 in that project, and `#sec-9` narrows it
  to one section. The same pattern with `ADR` instead of `SPEC` points at an
  architecture decision record.
- **`WL-123`** is a task id: project key, then a per-project number.
